title: Choosing the right life cycle
blurb: Compare linear, iterative, hybrid and extended life cycles, pick the right one for a scenario and never mix up their phase names.
question: A housing association has four projects: new roofs to a fixed specification, a tenant portal nobody can yet specify, a community hub with a booking app shaped by residents, and a repairs system whose savings the board wants proven after handover. Which life cycle suits each?

teach.body: Every project needs a life cycle, but not the same one. The main question is how stable and well understood the requirements are. Stable: linear. Evolving: iterative. A mix of both in one project: hybrid. And if the life cycle must keep going after handover until the benefits in the business case are realised, use the extended life cycle. Choosing well gives control where it helps and flexibility where it is needed.

teach.h: Which life cycle? A quick decision

root.label: Are the requirements stable and well understood?

teach.caption: Then ask: must the life cycle run on until benefits are realised? If so, extend a linear life cycle with Adoption and Benefits realisation.

teach.body: Roof replacement on 200 homes to an agreed specification: requirements are stable, so linear. A tenant self-service portal nobody can yet describe: iterative, with tenants reviewing each time box. A community hub built to fixed drawings with a booking app shaped by residents: hybrid. A new repairs system whose savings the board wants proven after handover: extended, adding Adoption and Benefits realisation.

teach.text: The exam swaps names between models. Check every name: Concept, Definition and Transition are linear (and so also extended). Feasibility, Foundations and Evolutionary development are iterative only. Deployment is in both. Adoption and Benefits realisation are extended only. Words like Implementation, Handover and closure, Operations or Termination are not BoK 7 phase names.

teach.h: Exam technique for life cycle questions
items: Spot the clue words: 'stable' means linear, 'time boxes' or 'feedback' means iterative.
'Combines' or 'mixes' means hybrid; 'after handover' or 'benefits' means extended.
In a list of phases, check every single name belongs to the model asked about.
Then check the order: Concept before Definition, Feasibility before Foundations.
Linear: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. Suits stable requirements.
Iterative: Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment. Suits evolving requirements.
Hybrid: combines linear and iterative approaches within one project.
Extended: linear plus Adoption and Benefits realisation, running until benefits are realised.
Never put Concept, Definition or Transition in an iterative list.

summary: You can now compare all four life cycle models, state each one's phases in order, and choose the right model for a scenario. You can also catch the swapped phase names the exam uses to trip candidates up.

A.q: Which life cycle best suits a project whose requirements are stable and fully understood from the start?
A.why: Stable, well-understood requirements suit a linear life cycle: plan fully, then build in one pass.

whyNot.0: Iterative suits evolving requirements that need repeated feedback.
whyNot.1: Hybrid is for projects where only some parts are stable.
whyNot.3: Extended is about continuing until benefits are realised, not about stable requirements.

A.q: Users of a new research database can't say what they need until they have tried early versions. Which life cycle fits best?
A.why: When requirements only emerge through use, iterative time boxes with user feedback fit best.

whyNot.1: Linear needs requirements defined up front, which these users can't do.
whyNot.2: Extended adds phases after handover; it doesn't address unclear requirements.
whyNot.3: Nothing here is stable enough to need a linear strand, so a hybrid isn't required.

A.q: Which phase name is found ONLY in the extended life cycle?
A.why: Adoption (with Benefits realisation) is what the extended life cycle adds after Transition.

whyNot.0: Deployment appears in both the linear and the iterative models.
whyNot.2: Definition is a linear phase, so it appears in the extended life cycle but not only there.

B.q: Which sequence mixes phase names from two different models?
B.why: Definition is a linear phase; it doesn't belong between Feasibility and Evolutionary development, which are iterative.

whyNot.0: This is the correct linear sequence.
whyNot.2: This is the correct iterative sequence.
whyNot.3: These are the last three phases of the extended life cycle, all from one model.

B.q: Which statement correctly matches a life cycle to its key feature?
options: Linear: phases repeat in time boxes
Iterative: scope flexes, time is fixed
B.why: In an iterative life cycle, time and cost are fixed per time box and scope flexes.

whyNot.0: Repeating time boxes is iterative; linear runs once, in order.
whyNot.1: Adding Adoption after Transition is the extended life cycle.
whyNot.3: Mixing linear and iterative is the hybrid life cycle.

B.q: Which option correctly pairs the FIRST phase of each model?
B.why: The linear life cycle starts with Concept; the iterative life cycle starts with Feasibility.

whyNot.0: This swaps the two models' first phases.
whyNot.1: Foundations is the SECOND iterative phase.
whyNot.2: Definition is the SECOND linear phase.

C.q:
Which TWO factors point towards an iterative life cycle?
1) Requirements are likely to change
2) Users can give frequent feedback
3) Scope is fixed by the contract
4) Each phase must finish before the next
C.why: Changing requirements and users available for frequent feedback are exactly what iterative working needs.

whyNot.1: User feedback suits iterative, but scope fixed by contract points to linear.
whyNot.2: Fixed scope and strictly sequential phases both point to linear.
whyNot.3: Changing requirements suit iterative, but finishing each phase before the next is linear.

C.q: Kestrel must replace roofs on 200 homes to an agreed specification, and its board wants proof after handover that heating complaints have fallen. Which life cycle fits best?
C.why: The roof work is stable (linear), and proving benefits after handover means adding Adoption and Benefits realisation: an extended life cycle.

whyNot.0: Nothing here needs iterative working, so there is nothing to mix: running on to benefits is extension, not hybrid.
whyNot.2: The specification is agreed, so iterative time boxes aren't needed.
whyNot.3: A plain linear life cycle ends at Transition, before the complaint figures can be proven.

C.q: Which statement about the number of phases is correct?
C.why: Linear and iterative each have four phases; extended adds two (Adoption and Benefits realisation) to the four linear ones, making six.

whyNot.1: The iterative life cycle has four phases, not five.
whyNot.2: Linear has four phases, not five, and extended has six, not seven.
whyNot.3: Extended adds TWO phases, so it has six.

reteach.title: Choosing how to plan a holiday
reteach.question: A package tour, a backpacking trip, a city break with free days, and a fitness retreat whose real payoff comes weeks later. Which life cycle is each like?

blocks.body: A package tour is booked in full before you leave and followed in order: linear. Backpacking is planned a few days at a time, adjusting as you learn: iterative. A city break with fixed flights and hotel but free days to decide as you go: hybrid. A fitness retreat isn't a success when you fly home, but weeks later when the new habits have stuck: extended.

blocks.text: Hybrid is about HOW you deliver (mixing). Extended is about HOW LONG the life cycle runs (until benefits).

explain.body: Choose linear when requirements are stable and well understood, change is unlikely and the work must be done in a fixed order, such as construction to an agreed design.

test.q: Which project is the best fit for a linear life cycle?
options: A game refined with player input
A car park resurfaced to a set design
An app whose features users will shape
A website rebuild with unclear needs
test.why: Resurfacing to a set design has stable, well-understood requirements, which suits linear.

whyNot.0: Refining with player feedback is iterative.
whyNot.3: Unclear needs point to iterative working.

explain.body: Choose iterative when requirements are uncertain or likely to change, users can give frequent feedback, and early value matters. Time and cost are fixed per time box; scope flexes.

explain.loop: Evolutionary development repeats in time boxes

test.q: In which situation would a linear life cycle struggle most?
options: The scope is fixed by contract
test.why: Linear needs requirements fixed up front; constantly changing needs suit an iterative life cycle instead.

whyNot.0: An agreed design is ideal for linear.

explain.body: Choose hybrid when one project contains both stable and uncertain work, or when governance wants a firm linear business case and baseline but delivery needs iterative feedback.

test.q: Which project most needs a hybrid life cycle?
options: A road resurfaced to a fixed design
A game refined sprint by sprint
A stadium build plus a fan-led app
A system tracked for later savings
test.why: A fixed stadium build (linear) with an app shaped by fans (iterative) in one project is a hybrid.

whyNot.3: Tracking savings after handover points to an extended life cycle.

explain.body: Choose extended when the life cycle must run on after Transition, through Adoption and Benefits realisation, until the benefits in the business case are realised.

test.q: Which need points most clearly to an extended life cycle?
test.why: Running on after handover until benefits are proven is the purpose of the extended life cycle.

whyNot.3: Fixing scope before the build is linear.
